subject: Chemistry
title: Haloalkanes and Haloarenes
summary: In haloalkanes the C–X bond is polar (Cδ⁺–Xδ⁻), so the carbon is attacked by nucleophiles. Reactivity of R–X: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl > R–F (weaker bond, better leaving group).
Nucleophilic substitution goes by SN2 (one step, backside attack, inversion, favoured by 1° halides) or SN1 (carbocation, racemisation, favoured by 3° halides and polar protic solvents).
With alcoholic KOH, haloalkanes undergo elimination (dehydrohalogenation) to alkenes; the more substituted alkene is the major product (Saytzeff rule).
Haloarenes are much less reactive to nucleophiles (partial C=X double bond from resonance, sp² carbon). They undergo electrophilic substitution at ortho/para positions.

formulas.name: From alcohols
formulas.formula: ROH + HX (ZnCl₂ for HCl) → RX;  ROH + PCl₅/PCl₃/SOCl₂ → RCl
formulas.note: SOCl₂ is best: by-products SO₂ and HCl are gases, leaving pure RCl.

formulas.name: SN2 mechanism
formulas.formula: rate = k[RX][Nu⁻];  one step;  inversion (Walden);  CH₃X > 1° > 2° > 3°
formulas.when: Primary halides with strong nucleophiles in aprotic solvents.
formulas.note: Steric hindrance stops SN2 at 3° carbons.

formulas.name: Nucleophilicity in a polar protic solvent
formulas.formula: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻;   RO⁻ > C₆H₅O⁻;   e.g. towards CH₃Br in methanol: I⁻ > C₂H₅O⁻ > C₆H₅O⁻ > F⁻
formulas.note: Small, hard anions (F⁻) are held tightly by H-bonding to the solvent, so they react slowly; phenoxide is weaker than ethoxide because its charge is delocalised into the ring. In aprotic solvents (DMSO, acetone) the halide order reverses: F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻.

formulas.name: SN1 mechanism
formulas.formula: rate = k[RX];  carbocation intermediate;  racemisation;  3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃X
formulas.when: Tertiary/benzylic/allylic halides in polar protic solvents.

formulas.name: Elimination (dehydrohalogenation)
formulas.formula: R–CH₂–CH₂X + alc. KOH → R–CH=CH₂ + KX + H₂O
formulas.note: Aqueous KOH → substitution (alcohol); alcoholic KOH → elimination (alkene).

formulas.name: Saytzeff (Zaitsev) rule
formulas.formula: the more substituted alkene is the major product of elimination

formulas.name: Ambident nucleophiles
formulas.formula: KCN → R–CN (alkyl cyanide);  AgCN → R–NC (isocyanide);  KNO₂ → R–ONO;  AgNO₂ → R–NO₂

formulas.name: Grignard reagent
formulas.formula: R–X + Mg (dry ether) → RMgX;  RMgX + H₂O → R–H
formulas.note: Must be kept dry — any water (or –OH, –NH) destroys it.

formulas.name: Nucleophilic substitution in haloarenes
formulas.formula: needs drastic conditions (Dow's process: 623 K, 300 atm) unless –NO₂ groups are at ortho/para
formulas.note: o/p-NO₂ groups make it much easier; meta-NO₂ has little effect.

examples.title: SN1 or SN2?
examples.problem: Which reacts faster with OH⁻ by SN2: CH₃Br or (CH₃)₃CBr?
examples.solution: CH₃Br — no steric hindrance for the backside attack. (CH₃)₃CBr reacts by SN1 instead, through a stable 3° carbocation.

examples.title: Stereochemistry
examples.problem: (R)-2-bromobutane reacts with OH⁻ by SN2. Product?
examples.solution: (S)-butan-2-ol: SN2 inverts the configuration. By SN1 a nearly racemic mixture would form.

examples.title: Major alkene
examples.solution: But-2-ene (more substituted) is major (Saytzeff); but-1-ene is minor.

examples.title: KCN vs AgCN
examples.problem: CH₃CH₂Br with KCN and with AgCN?
examples.solution: KCN (ionic, C attacks) → CH₃CH₂CN; AgCN (covalent, N attacks) → CH₃CH₂NC.

examples.title: Why is chlorobenzene unreactive?
examples.problem: Explain why chlorobenzene resists nucleophilic substitution.
examples.solution: Resonance gives the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character, the carbon is sp² (holds electrons tightly), the phenyl cation is unstable, and the electron-rich ring repels nucleophiles.

examples.title: Finkelstein
examples.problem: Convert ethyl chloride to ethyl iodide.
examples.solution: Heat with NaI in dry acetone: C₂H₅Cl + NaI → C₂H₅I + NaCl (NaCl precipitates, driving the reaction).

topics.title: Classification and nomenclature
topics.explain: Mono-, di-, polyhalo compounds; alkyl (1°, 2°, 3°), allylic, benzylic, vinylic and aryl halides. Vinylic and aryl halides have X on an sp² carbon and are unreactive in SN reactions.

topics.title: Physical properties
topics.explain: Boiling points rise with size of halogen (RI > RBr > RCl > RF) and chain length, and fall with branching. Haloalkanes are only slightly soluble in water. p-Dichlorobenzene melts higher than the o- and m-isomers (symmetrical, packs better).

topics.title: Factors deciding SN1 vs SN2
topics.explain: Substrate: 1° → SN2, 3° → SN1, 2° → both. Strong nucleophiles and aprotic solvents favour SN2; weak nucleophiles and polar protic solvents (water, alcohols) favour SN1. Benzylic and allylic halides react fast by SN1 (resonance-stabilised carbocations). Bridgehead halides (1-bromobicyclo[2.2.2]octane, 1-bromonorbornane) react extremely slowly by SN1 — the rigid cage cannot let the carbocation become planar; the more strained norbornyl is the slowest. At the other end, (C₆H₅)₃C⁺ is very stable (three rings share the charge), so trityl halides are fastest.

topics.title: Optical activity basics
topics.explain: A chiral molecule (carbon with four different groups) is non-superimposable on its mirror image and rotates plane-polarised light. Enantiomers rotate equally in opposite directions; a 50:50 mixture (racemic) is optically inactive.

topics.title: Electrophilic substitution in haloarenes
topics.explain: Halogen is deactivating but o/p-directing: chlorobenzene gives o- and p-products in halogenation, nitration, sulphonation and Friedel–Crafts reactions (p major).

topics.title: Polyhalogen compounds and environment
topics.explain: CH₂Cl₂ (solvent), CHCl₃ (chloroform, once an anaesthetic; stored in dark bottles because it forms poisonous phosgene in light), CHI₃ (iodoform, antiseptic), CCl₄ (solvent, harms the ozone layer), freons (CFCs, refrigerants, ozone depletion) and DDT (insecticide, persists in food chains).

ratta: SN2: 1°, inversion, one step;  SN1: 3°, racemisation, carbocation.
Aq. KOH → alcohol;  alc. KOH → alkene (Saytzeff).
KCN → RCN;  AgCN → RNC;  KNO₂ → RONO;  AgNO₂ → RNO₂.
Protic solvent: I⁻ > C₂H₅O⁻ > C₆H₅O⁻ > F⁻ (F⁻ most solvated).
SN1: Ph₃C–X fastest;  bridgehead halides very slow (no planar carbocation).
